title: DfE Decoded #169: Parental Engagement Matters, But Not in the Way We Sometimes Think
author: Paul Urry
summary: Urry reads the DfE's new longitudinal research on parental engagement and argues that quality matters more than intensity. Quiet, ordinary forms of engagement, such as books at home, library visits, conversation, reading for enjoyment and clear information about progress, track better outcomes than frequent teacher contact or heavy homework involvement, which often signal an existing problem. He repeatedly cautions against reading correlation as causation, for example with parents teaching letters or homework hours. He argues that parental engagement policy can slide into parental blame, and that capacity to engage is unequally distributed. His leadership advice is to make engagement easier: clearer communication, accessible parents' evenings, simple home messages and high expectations for every pathway.
points: Reactive, frequent contact with school is usually a symptom of difficulty, whereas clear routine communication is associated with stronger outcomes.
Conversation, reading and library use build language-rich homes, and homework sheets do not.
Parental expectations of continued learning, including apprenticeships, are among the strongest associations with attainment.
Engagement strategies that rely on time, money or confidence risk widening gaps, so schools should design for the hardest-to-reach families.
quotes: Parental engagement is not one thing. And more involvement does not automatically mean better outcomes.
So more contact does not necessarily cause poorer outcomes. It may simply be a sign that there was already a problem.
Language-rich homes are not created through homework sheets. They are created through interaction.
Because schools often confuse more communication with better communication.
A desk is not a study habit. A laptop is not engagement. A bookshelf is not reading.
Because parental engagement policy can easily become parental blame.
The strongest partnerships are not built around compliance. They are built around a shared understanding that school and family are trying to achieve the same thing.
